title: How Indian Festivals Turn the Seasons Into a Way of Eating
excerpt: From til-gur sweets in January to Navratri fasts and Diwali mithai in autumn, the festival calendar follows the harvest — and still sets the menu for families abroad.
body:
• India's festival calendar tracks the agricultural year: harvest festivals such as Makar Sankranti, Pongal and Baisakhi are built around the crop that has just come in.
  • Fasting and feasting alternate by season — Navratri's nine days of fruit, nuts and buckwheat or millet flours in autumn, Janmashtami fasts in the humid monsoon, and ghee-and-nut sweets at Diwali to build warmth before winter.
  • Winter festivals centre on sesame and jaggery — til-gur sweets at Lohri and Makar Sankranti — foods eaten for warmth in the coldest months.
  • For diaspora families, the same calendar still sets the menu abroad: an Onam sadya, a Pongal pot or a Diwali mithai box marks the season even where the local weather does not change with it.

An Indian festival rarely arrives with a random menu. The dishes are set by the season in which the festival falls and by the crop that season has just produced — a pattern that runs from a Tamil Pongal pot in January to a Punjabi Lohri fire the same week.

The harvest sets the table

A large share of the festival calendar is agricultural at its core. Makar Sankranti and Pongal, in mid-January, mark the sun's turn and the rice harvest; the food is rice — sakkarai pongal, sweetened with jaggery, moong dal and ghee, and its savoury counterpart ven pongal with black pepper and cumin. Baisakhi in mid-April celebrates the rabi harvest in Punjab — wheat and mustard sown in winter — with sarson da saag and makki di roti. Onam in Kerala, in August-September, is served as the sadya: a vegetarian feast of 20 or more dishes on a banana leaf, eaten in a set order. As a guide to India's food culture puts it, a festival dish made with freshly harvested jaggery, sesame or rice is not a coincidence — it is what is abundant at that exact moment in the agricultural year, which is why the same festival produces different dishes in different states.

"The harvest sets the table A large share of the festival calendar is agricultural at its core."

Fasting in one season, feasting in the next

The calendar also alternates restraint with abundance, in step with the weather. In spring, Holi follows the heavy eating of winter with gujiyas and thandai, a chilled spiced milk drink. The monsoon months bring fasts — Janmashtami observances rest the digestion in humid weather, broken later with butter, milk and nuts — and Teej's greens. Autumn's Navratri keeps a nine-day fast on fruits, nuts and gluten-free grains or millets such as sabudana and kuttu, before Diwali reverses the direction: sweets with nuts and ghee that provide warmth and energy for the winter ahead, according to a season-by-season account of festival eating. Winter itself is warming food: sesame, jaggery and peanuts at Lohri bonfires, and til-gur sweets at Sankranti.

Six tastes, one plate

Underneath the festivals sits an everyday structure that makes seasonal eating easy to sustain: the thali, a single platter carrying a grain, a dal, vegetables, curd or raita, a pickle and something sweet, designed to hold all six tastes recognised in Indian food philosophy — sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent and astringent. Ugadi and Gudi Padwa, the spring new-year festivals, make the same point in a single chutney that combines all six tastes at once. Religion layers its own rules over the seasons: Jain cooking that skips root vegetables, Ramzan fasts broken with dates and sheer khurma, and the Sikh langar, a free vegetarian meal served to anyone who enters a gurdwara.

What survives the move abroad

For Indian families overseas, the festival calendar often outlasts the climate it was designed for. A sadya assembled in Toronto or a box of Diwali mithai exchanged in New Jersey still marks the turn of a season that the local weather may not announce. What changes is the sourcing — frozen banana leaves, imported jaggery, sweet shops taking the place of a week of home mithai-making — and, increasingly, the recording: families now document festival recipes in blogs and videos that earlier generations passed on only by word of mouth. The structure, though, is intact: fast when the tradition says fast, feast on what the harvest festival names, and let the calendar, not the supermarket, decide what is for dinner.
